sources.title: Rack up Wins With the Nimzowitsch-Larsen Attack
Search snippet: Nimzo-Larsen 1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.e3 results (Wikipedia, Chess.com forums, TheChessWorld, KingSights)

overview: White plays 1.b3 and, after 1...e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.e3, lets Black build a classical e5/d5 centre and aims to undermine it with the Bb2 on the long diagonal plus Bb5, Nf3, f4, c4 and a knight on e5 or d4. The main line runs 3...d5 4.Bb5 Bd6, where White holds the dark squares and presses on e5. Wikipedia calls this true hypermodern style; opening theory generally rates many 1.b3 lines only equal, but White often gains practical chances because Black does not know the reversed-colour positions. Play is usually quiet and manoeuvring with a broad Black pawn centre to be targeted, though f4 and kingside pawn storms can give an attacking flavour. It is used by Bent Larsen, Nakamura and Carlsen mostly as a surprise weapon in blitz.

white_ideas.idea: Fianchetto Bb2 to press e5/long diagonal, then e3 and Bb5 to pin/pressure the c6 knight and d4 square
Dark-square strategy with Bb2, e3, Bb5, f4, Nf3 and Ne5
Counterattack the broad Black pawn centre with c4 and f4 breaks, attacking its defenders
Optionally castle queenside combined with g4-h4 pawn storms

black_ideas.idea: Establish a classical e5/d5 pawn centre and develop comfortably (Nc6, Nf6, Bd6)
Guard g7 and the long diagonal against Bb2; keep central control
Equalise with accurate play; vary with 2...d6 (English-like) or 2...f5 (Ringelbach)

typical_structures.structure: Black pawns on e5 and d5 against a flank-developed White: Bb2, pawn e3 and c-pawn possibly c4, the Larsen 'reversed' set-up

character.notes: Described as 'true hypermodern': White allows a classical Black centre and undermines it; USCF Sales calls it positionally sound and giving calm, principled middlegames. Not forcing; plans are manoeuvring (Bb5, c4, f4). Occasional f4/g4 pawn storms add some attacking potential. Black can meet it comfortably and equalise.

gambit.notes: No material is given in the main line. Sideline: Ringelbach Gambit (1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 f5 3.e4), a rare Black gambit-like line in the subtree.

soundness.notes: Wikipedia: many 1.b3 lines are rated only equal by theory, but practitioners gain practical advantages at shorter time controls because of Black's unfamiliarity. Chess Doctrine: White may not exert enough pressure on the centre, so Black equalises with accurate play. USCF Sales: positionally sound, viable at elite level (2021 master games). Sound for White, with at most a small concession in objective terms.

structure.notes: Black's e5/d5 pawn centre faces a flank-based White; White's plan is to attack it with pieces and c4/f4. The centre is therefore in tension with pawns staying on until White breaks; roughly closed to semi-closed but can open after c4 or f4.

approach.notes: A flank opening: White plays b3 and Bb2 against nearly any reply (1...e5, 1...d5, 1...Nf6). Wikipedia says it is used by Larsen (its principal advocate), Nakamura and Carlsen as a surprise weapon in online blitz; Chess Doctrine says it is not played frequently at top level in classical chess but is used to avoid revealing repertoires. Respectable but a minority choice.

level.notes: Minimal theory: Chess Doctrine says it prioritises themes over strict lines; USCF Sales says confidence is possible after a weekend of study. Understanding reversed structures and when to play f4 or c4 is the demanding part.

plan_phrases: queenside castling with kingside pawn storm

sublines_that_differ.name: Main line 3...d5 4.Bb5 Bd6
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. b3 e5 2. Bb2 Nc6 3. e3 d5 4. Bb5 Bd6
sublines_that_differ.how: The standard hypermodern structure; White plans to undermine Black's centre.

sublines_that_differ.name: 2...d6
sublines_that_differ.how: Black keeps a solid pawn structure; White may follow with e3, Ne2 and d4/f4 or transpose to English with c4.

sublines_that_differ.name: Ringelbach Gambit
sublines_that_differ.how: Black attacks with ...f5; a sharp, rare line.

description.claim: White immediately cedes central pawn control to fight for it with pieces from the flank
description.note: Wikipedia: White allows a classical e5/d5 centre then undermines it.

description.claim: White's strategy revolves around the fianchettoed bishop on b2, aiming to undermine Black's central foothold
description.note: Bb2 on the long diagonal and the e5 pawn.

description.claim: The opening leads to strategically complex and unbalanced positions
description.note: Sources describe calm middlegames; 'unbalanced' is not borne out. Black can equalise.

common_plans.claim: White: fianchetto Bb2, control the e5 pawn, and challenge Black's centre with c4 or f4
common_plans.note: c4 and f4 breaks named by USCF Sales.

common_plans.claim: White: develop the kingside (Nf3, e3, Be2) and castle
common_plans.note: Nf3 and e3 appear; Be2 does not (Bb5 is the usual bishop move in the main line).

common_plans.claim: Black: solidify the centre with d5 and develop quickly (Nc6, Nf6)
Black: use the space advantage to launch an attack or restrict White's pieces
common_plans.note: Black seeks comfortable development and central control; no source describes a Black attack plan.

common_plans.claim: Black: challenge the fianchetto set-up by controlling the long diagonal or a kingside pawn storm
common_plans.note: Guarding g7 and the long diagonal appears in Chess Doctrine; a Black pawn storm was not found.
